Comment.MultiLanguageText: The position source normalised so TRUE always means PROVEN OPEN, whichever state the source is wired to prove. Named once here because both detections, the enable, the cycle count and the status code all read it (C-601), and because the sense question then has exactly one answer in the block.
One scan on the rising edge of a debounced proven-open operation, for the cycle counter. The live half of C-404's explicit edge construction.
The debounced proven-open state as it was last scan. The stored half of C-404's edge construction; nothing else may read it.
The fail-to preset in milliseconds, derived once from the operator-facing seconds figure. BOTH fail-to timers share it, which is what makes them one setting rather than two free to drift apart.
The upstream-enable preset in milliseconds, derived once from the operator-facing seconds figure.

AttributeList.Text: GENERIC TWO-STATE VALVE. One energised state that OPENS and one de-energised state that CLOSES, the de-energised state being the fail-safe: there is no close command, the output dropping IS the close, and the valve fails shut with no energy on it. WRITTEN AS A LIBRARY BLOCK. It is deliberately over-specified against any single application - it carries capability a given plant will never exercise - because stripping a proven capability out is cheap and discovering a missing one at commissioning is not. Nothing in it names a plant, a process, a fluid, a vessel or an alarm register; everything site-specific belongs to how an instance is WIRED, never to the block. INTERFACE PER C-132: the entire caller-visible interface is the single STATIC IO of type UDT_Valve, and the block declares no INPUT, OUTPUT or IN_OUT parameters at all. The instance DB IS the interface - the caller writes into it, the panel binds to it, and RETAIN can be stated here because this is the only place it can be stated at all. C-132's cost is real and its mitigation is the CALLER'S obligation, not this block's: the call site shows nothing, so whoever calls this block must put its writes to an instance's struct IMMEDIATELY ADJACENT to that instance's CALL, never scattered. A reviewer who cannot see the writes beside the call should treat that as a finding. STRUCTURE IS patterns/motor-dol'S, DELIBERATELY. A DOL motor and a two-state valve are the same problem in different clothes, so the member names, the network order and the seal-in discipline are carried across rather than re-invented, and where the motor's shape did not transfer the network that would have carried it says so. WHAT WAS DROPPED, ON THE OWNER'S RULING: the prestart apparatus and the hand-selector edges that serve it; the controlled-shutdown apparatus; the hand-intervention latch and recent-start memory, because the hand command here is MAINTAINED rather than a momentary press; and the seal-in on the command itself, which in the motor exists to bypass the prestart permissives once running and has nothing left to bypass once prestart is gone - so it is not carried across as decoration. ONE FAIL-TO TIME SERVES BOTH DIRECTIONS, exactly as the motor shares one preset across fail-to-run and fail-to-stop. PROVING, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST. The block takes a COMPUTED position Bool and does not know what produced it - a real limit contact, or an inference the caller draws from any process variable it likes, arrive on the same member. That is what keeps this a library block rather than one plant's block: thresholds, windows, magnitudes and attribution all live in whatever computes that Bool, and none of them is built in here. C-131 GOVERNS BOTH DETECTIONS WITHOUT EXCEPTION: a feedback proves NON-ARRIVAL and never proves arrival, so both fire on POSITIVE EVIDENCE OF THE WRONG STATE - commanded open and the position says not open, commanded shut and the position says still open - and neither fires on the absence of evidence of the right one. A QUIET FEEDBACK IS NEVER READ AS A SEALED VALVE. C-131's third state, cannot-tell, is carried explicitly as PositionValid; it GATES whether a fault may arm and is never read as a position in either direction. WHAT THIS BLOCK IS NOT, AND THE GAPS ARE NAMED RATHER THAN GUESSED: it holds no interlock that reads a SIBLING device, because a block cannot see its siblings; it does not re-drive itself to a required state after a power failure or a safety stop, which is a sequencing decision and not a valve decision; it does not decide how it learns that its process is simulated; and it does not interpret the suppressor encoding it publishes. Each of those is the caller's, and each is listed as an open point rather than answered here, because a plausible answer written into a block is worse than a named gap. RETENTION: IO carries RETAIN SETPOINT as the motor's own does. That retains the whole struct including the derived alarm word, which costs a few bytes and no correctness - the word is rewritten every scan and is therefore not a second seal-in - while the alternative loses a latched critical fault across a power cycle. NOTE FOR WHOEVER OWNS THE MEMORY BUDGET: under C-132 the ENTIRE interface of every equipment instance is retentive, which is a materially different figure from retaining a handful of fault bits, and it wants re-running before this shape is committed across every equipment class.

The motor pattern's source-selection and fail-safe rung, reduced to what a valve needs. THE TWO COMMAND SOURCES REPLACE EACH OTHER RATHER THAN COMBINING, so there is no state in which both partly drive the valve and no order of events that leaves the operator and the sequence disagreeing about who has it. The command then passes an external inhibit, the block's OWN fault condensation, and a system-healthy permissive; any of the three de-energises the valve whatever either source is asking for. THE FAIL-SAFE IS THE MOTOR'S, CARRIED OVER UNCHANGED - a device that has just reported it is not doing what it was told is not a device to keep driving - and on this block de-energising is the safe direction by construction. NO SEAL-IN, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE RATHER THAN AN OMISSION: the motor seals its own run bit in order to BYPASS its prestart and recent-start permissives once running, and with the prestart apparatus dropped there is nothing left to bypass, so a seal-in here would be decoration that also defeated the inhibit terms it sat outside. ONE COIL AND NOT TWO, for the same reason - the motor's separate try-run bit differs from its run bit only by that seal-in and the shutdown terms, and with both gone the two would be identical every scan, which is the duplication C-409 exists to prevent. INTERLOCKS THAT READ SIBLING VALVES ARRIVE THROUGH InhibitValve: a block cannot see its siblings, and the logic that can belongs to whoever owns them. READS ITS OWN FAULT BIT FROM THE PREVIOUS SCAN, exactly as the motor does; the one-scan lag on closing is immaterial against any actuator travel time.
Valve Open / Close

The operator-facing times on the interface are Real SECONDS for legibility; the timers below need their PT as a DInt millisecond value. One multiply-and-convert pair per preset, in order: FTTime to FTTimeMS - ONE preset shared by both fail-to timers, exactly as the motor shares one across fail-to-run and fail-to-stop - then EnableUPSTime to EnableUPSTimeMS. Kept as one block up front rather than repeated at each timer, so the times-a-thousand idiom is visibly consistent and only ever done once (C-126 documented exception). THE PAIRING IS BY INDEX, NOT BY ADJACENCY: every multiply renders in one contiguous run and every convert in the next, so the first convert takes the first multiply's result and the second takes the second's.
HMI Times

Which state the position source proves is a WIRING FACT, and it is answered once, here, rather than being asserted in the name of every signal that carries it - so the opposite wiring costs a setting and not a code change, and there is one place to look when the answer turns out to have been wrong. Everything downstream reads proven-open and never has to remember the sense.
Position Feedback, Normalised To Prove Open

C-131 IN ITS PLAINEST FORM: this fires on POSITIVE EVIDENCE OF THE WRONG STATE - the valve was commanded open, the position source is trustworthy, and it says the valve is not open - and it never fires on the absence of evidence of the right state. ARMED FROM A COMMAND THE PROGRAM ITSELF ISSUED, which is what C-131 asks for: the valve was TOLD to change state, so a window opens in which its effect must appear, and that is certain knowledge where arming from an inference would be one more thing that can be wrong. PositionValid is C-131's cannot-tell state and it REMOVES the detection rather than degrading it - on a valve with no position source of any kind it is permanently false and this fault can never raise, which is the honest answer for a valve nobody can judge. THE SEAL-IN IS ON THIS BIT AT THIS NETWORK and it is the only seal-in for this fact anywhere in the block (C-508); the alarm bit downstream is a direct unlatched read of it.
Fail To Open

The mirror of the network above, and the more important of the two. IT PROVES THE VALVE DID NOT CLOSE - the position source still says open - AND IT NEVER PROVES THAT IT DID. A quiet feedback is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence: the actuator could have stalled between limits, the seat could be holding on debris that will shift, the sensor could have failed low. So a valve nobody can currently judge leaves this fault QUIET rather than CLEAR, and the difference between those two is what the published suppressor cause exists to tell an operator. Same shared preset as the open direction, on the owner's ruling that two presets are not worth the divergence they invite.
Fail To Close

The external fault input, held until reset, on the same seal-in shape as the two detections above. IT IS A CAUSE BIT OF ITS OWN RATHER THAN A RESET COIL ON THE INPUT, which is where this departs from the motor pattern and does so on purpose: latching the caller's own input in place would give that member two writers - the caller who raises it and this block which clears it - where a separate cause bit leaves it with one, and puts this fact's seal-in at a detection network like every other cause (C-508).
External Fault Latch

A pure OR of the three latched causes with NO SEAL-IN OF ITS OWN - every term is already sealed at its own detection network, and a second seal here is the duplicate C-508 forbids. The motor pattern does seal this bit, and that is the one place this block knowingly departs from it: C-508 was corrected on 06/08/2026 to put the seal on the cause and not on the condensation, and the pattern predates the correction. ITS POSITION UPSTREAM OF THE ALARM-WRITE NETWORKS IS WHAT MAKES SUPPRESSION SAFE - the panel can be emptied and this bit cannot - and it is what network 1 reads for its fail-safe, so the valve closing itself on its own fault is not defeatable by suppression either. The standing in-hand indication is deliberately not a term.
Faults

The first of two consequence classes, for applications whose severity scheme separates a fault that must drop outputs and freeze from one that need only freeze the step in progress. MEMBERSHIP HERE IS A PROPERTY OF THE INSTANCE AND NOT OF THE MEMBER, which is unusual and is the reason the interface carries a configuration bit for it at all: the same physical condition - a valve still passing while shut - is a nuisance on one duty and a hazard on another, so the class is told to the block rather than inferred by it. Where that bit is clear this one is permanently clear, which is a TRUE STATEMENT ABOUT THAT INSTANCE and not a gap. Pure OR, no seal-in, upstream of every suppression term, so a suppressed critical fault still drops outputs.
Critical Class Consequence

The second consequence class and the exact complement of the network above: a failure to open is the lesser class wherever it is detected, a failure to close is the lesser class only where it is not the greater one, and an external fault is the lesser class always. WHAT FEEDS NEITHER CLASS BIT: the in-hand indication, which is a deliberate act and must not freeze anything. Between them the two bits partition every latched cause with none left over, so the condensation in network 7 is provably identical to their OR on every instance - a property a reviewer can check by reading three networks, recorded rather than exploited, because writing it a third way would give one fact three homes.
Error Class Consequence

A STANDING CONDITION AND NOT A FAULT: no seal-in, no clearing on reset, and it feeds neither the fault condensation nor either consequence bit. It is a direct read of the mode bit, so the fact that this valve is in hand has exactly one home and the alarm word carries a view of it rather than a second copy.
Valve In Hand

The C-115 handshake out. IT REQUIRES POSITIVE PROOF AND DOES NOT ASSUME IT - the valve must be commanded open AND the position source must say it is open - so a valve with no position source never enables. That is the conservative answer and the right one for a permissive whose failure mode is a downstream device starting into a shut valve. The block's own fault also drops the enable, so nothing it feeds keeps running on a valve that has reported itself faulty.
Valve Proven Open, Enable Upstream Component

Counted on an explicitly constructed rising edge - the debounced state compared against its stored previous scan, then the stored copy updated - because C-404 forbids the built-in edge instruction and C-401 forbids counter instructions. THE TWO COILS MUST STAY IN THIS ORDER: the edge is computed from last scan's stored copy and the copy is updated after it, and swapping them gives an edge that never fires. THE DEBOUNCE IS A FIXED CONSTANT AND NOT A SETTING, deliberately - it exists only so a chattering position source cannot inflate a wear count, it is far shorter than any real actuator stroke, and making it tunable would invite its being tuned into a second fail-to time. Rollover follows the motor pattern's own totaliser: at the ceiling the move to zero runs first and the add then takes it to one on the same scan.
Valve Operation Counter

The motor pattern's telemetry rung in valve form. A CHAIN OF OVERRIDING MOVES EXECUTED IN LISTED ORDER, LAST ENABLED WINS, which is why the fault case is last and why adding a state is one line rather than a re-cut of a comparison tree. The codes: -1 faulted, 0 closed, 1 commanded open and travelling, 2 proven open. THERE IS NO SEPARATE IN-HAND CODE - two covers proven open whether it was reached by hand or by the automatic source, because the in-hand fact is published on its own bit and a status code that also carried it would give one fact two homes and force every reader to decode a combination.
Valve Status Telemetry

THE ONE NETWORK THAT WRITES THIS WORD, and no other network writes any bit of it (C-501). A network's subject is the one variable it changes, and for an alarm network that variable is the WORD - so the alarm texts live here in the comment rather than in a title, because a word-sized network has nowhere else to put them. EVERY BIT IS A SINGLE NAMED CAUSE, NEVER AN INLINE EXPRESSION, which is what makes the slice access readable: you read the cause and know what the bit is, so the bit number never has to be decoded to understand the rung. EVERY BIT IS ALSO A DIRECT, UNLATCHED READ of a cause that is already latched at its own detection network - the alarm INHERITS latched behaviour by reading a latched bit and does not implement it, and there is exactly one seal-in per fact in this block, none of them here (C-508). THE SUPPRESSOR AND-TERMS ARE THE ONLY PLACE SUPPRESSION REACHES. Control reads FaultActive, which is written upstream in network 7, so filtering changes WHAT THE OPERATOR IS SHOWN and can never change WHAT THE PLANT DOES - a suppressed fault still closes this valve and still holds whatever the caller holds. THE BIT MAP: %X0 = FTO = <Valve> - failed to open - check the valve, its supply and the equipment that moves it. %X1 = FTC = <Valve> - still open when commanded shut - check the actuator and the seat; where two valves are separated by magnitude alone the site text must also carry the known misattribution, because a leak too small for the more severe threshold is reported against the less severe valve. %X2 = ExtFault = <Valve> - external actuator fault - check the actuator's own diagnostics. %X3 = OverrideActive = <Valve> - in hand - no action, released at the panel. BITS 4, 5 AND 6 ARE WRITTEN BY NO NETWORK IN THIS BLOCK and bits 7 to 15 are spare: an application may have vacated or reserved them, and this block writes only the four conditions it detects. WHY TWO OF THE FOUR HAVE NO SUPPRESSOR TERM: ExtFault reports a fault detected by something outside this block that already knows its own evidence, so no argument about a distrusted inference reaches it; and OverrideActive is itself commonly a SUPPRESSOR of other alarms, and an indication that suppresses others must not be capable of being hidden. In both cases the ABSENCE OF THE INPUT IS THE ENFORCEMENT - there is nothing there to wire wrongly.
Valve Alarm Word
